title: Yogachara Love Seeds
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett encourages listeners to explore how patterns of mind block their ability to give and receive love, using the Yogachara model as a tool for self-inquiry. By understanding how our minds generate reality and store experiences, tendencies, and impulses in a subconscious "storehouse consciousness," we can recognize when anxiety or negative thoughts arise and take a step back to observe them without identification. This recognition allows us to approach ourselves and others with compassion and understanding, rather than judgment or reaction, ultimately cultivating love and compassion in all aspects of life.

sentences.text: Good evening, everybody.
Welcome back, Scott.
It's good to be back.
It's so nice to be here with some space and some quiet, isn't it?
It's nice for me during this part of the evening to get to speak with you and say a few words.
Last week we had a ceremony of precepts, which is a certain kind of way to be together.
And the week before, Andrea Thatch gave a talk.
So I really appreciate getting to give the talk, or offer the talk.
And I appreciate you for receiving the talk, because it requires both of us, right?
It's worth noticing how rare this is: people getting together quietly, trying to speak carefully, trying to really listen to each other.
This is pretty rare, pretty wonderful.
I did listen to Andrea's talk.
If you weren't here, I recommend that you listen to her talk called Everything We Do Is About Love.
I'm happy to say that she's going to give the talk next week also, to continue the conversation.
She's also beginning a monthly study group starting tomorrow night.
It'll be on Thursday nights, once a month, at 7:15.
The exact Thursday night varies a little bit, so you need to sign up and put it in your calendar and everything.
Connected to this theme of love, I'm happy to say that our community is participating in an interfaith project with churches.
We're hanging with our Christian friends.
The project is called Let Love Be Our Legacy.
Its purpose is to bring attention to divisiveness, to judgment, to anger, and to the other possibilities, the other ways of being together.
We can be together with love.
Maybe you saw in the email that part of the project will be to open the Dharma Hall to the Bellingham community for meditation on Election Day.
Good idea, huh?
And the day after, like the recovery from Election Day.
Yeah, hopefully.
Or the sitting.
Well, the sitting with whatever it is, with whatever it is.
It's on the website, and it's a call for volunteers, too.
We're seeking volunteer hosts to help keep the Dharma Hall open on Election Day and the day after.
Hopefully somehow we'll manage to let the Bellingham community know, and other people will come who've never been here before.
Of course, it's all just a function of our mind, right?
Love, hate, war, peace.
We have these designations for these complicated minds, like Hillary Rodham Clinton and that other guy.
But it's really just the mind.
And so that's our project here, really, isn't it?
To understand the mind.
Conventionally we say to understand my mind, right?
To understand our mind as if the mind was something that we possessed and could control or understand exactly.
Maybe it is.
Maybe it's bigger or more subtle or more complex than anything that is ever going to quite fit into that box.
I wanted to share a little bit about what we investigated a couple of weekends ago.
We spent a weekend looking at one of the Buddhist models of the mind: the model from the Yogachara Buddhist school, the early Mahayana school, a fourth-, fifth-, sixth-century school of Buddhism.
As an independent school it mostly died out, but the ideas and thoughts they had permeate Mahayana Buddhism and permeate Zen.
I was thinking about those teachings in the light of this idea of love.
At first you don't really notice the love in Buddhist teachings.
In these Yogachara teachings, the word love is not mentioned in the text that we studied.
It's not explicitly there.
But if we think about what we mean by love, really, and what happens when that love is not present, we can wonder: what prevents it?
We all like love.
Who's not for love?
"Oh, I'm against love."
We're all for love.
But this is a little bit like our material well-being.
How come we're not always happy and in love with each other?
We've got so many things taken care of.
We're in such good shape in so many ways.
So it seems to come back again to the mind: there seem to be qualities of mind, habits of mind, patterns of mind that block love, that stop love, that bring up the opposite of love.
Of course, these are all just words.
What do we mean when we say love?
Four letters in English, one word; four letters in Spanish, too.
So there are maybe a lot of kinds of love.
I was thinking, what kind of love are we talking about when we say "everything we do is love" or "let love be our legacy"?
What kind of love would we like to be our legacy?
What kind of love would we like everything to be about?
Maybe a love that's open, but also a love that has some smarts to it, right?
A discerning kind of love.
Maybe it's a love that offers what's needed without holding back, but also a love that doesn't have anything extra in it.
You know those kinds of love that have all this extra stuff in them.
So maybe not that kind, but a wise love, an awakened love, if you will.
A love that truly helps.

So these teachings that we looked at from Yogachara Buddhism, these models of the mind, I was thinking, maybe these are a great way to study what blocks us from expressing and experiencing the wise love of Buddha.
And what's the path?
How do we nurture this love?
How do we allow it?
Although there seem to be some universal principles, more or less, and models that apply broadly, it does seem to come back to each of us, right?
Each of us has a different pattern, a different configuration, a different shape.
So let's think about this for ourselves for a minute.
What blocks your ability to give or receive love?
Give that a little turning over in your heart.
What blocks my natural human ability to give love, to receive love, this open, wise, pure love?
What's stopping you?
This Yogachara model, I find it really helpful.
Of course, it's just a model, right?
Reality is always bigger than models, even the wisest models.
But it's a good model, I think.
I think it can help us see some of the dynamics that block love or allow love, in a way that's both helpfully depersonalized and radically personal at the same time.
What do I mean by that?
We'll see if I can explain myself or not.
In some forms of its teaching, Yogachara says that everything that ever happens is a manifestation of the model of consciousness that they're going to present to us.
There's no external reality, as it were.
All of us, through our consciousness, are transforming and generating and creating everything that's happening for all of us together.
And there's a deep power to knowing and healing and learning about how this consciousness works.
It's not just a matter of cleaning things up or getting more in alignment with some objective reality that we've got a little distorted about and a little confused by.
It's actually that our consciousness itself is generating reality, is generating our lives.
That's pretty extreme, I guess.
But it's worth thinking about.
We have a very strong assumption, right?
A very, very powerful assumption that we'll probably never shake in this lifetime: that there's an external reality that's objective and the same for everybody.
It's just that we look at it differently.
And sometimes, well, I usually see it correctly, but other people are really pretty mixed up.
Or if your conditioning is the other way around: I'm never going to get this right and they all get it.
So now we have to back up a little bit.
The most important idea in the Yogachara model is really powerful and really feels right to me.
In this part of the model, they're trying to account for something.
They're trying to account for the way it seems like we're programmed by the past and by society.
Earlier Buddhist models emphasized the constant, changing, dynamic nature of everything: that everything arises together and influences itself and passes away.
And all models of Buddhism are very doubtful about the idea of the self.
The idea of the self as a fixed, rigid me, me, me, me, me that goes along over time and space is probably not really quite right.
But early Buddhism didn't really have a very good way of explaining why you suddenly remember something that your aunt told you when you were three, when you were trying to do something else.
It doesn't really explain things like racism either, or other kinds of prejudice and societal confusion.
I mean, it kind of does: the karma and the interactions of causes and effects and the web of all this is so rich and so vast and so endless that it just bubbles up that way.

But the Yogachara school said, no, there's a little more of something there that stores and holds onto all of these influences and memories and patterns and energies that we all seem to be walking around with, walking around in.
It accounts for the way things just bubble up.

Whether they bubble up consciously, like that memory of our aunt, or in a feeling way or an influence way, or we suddenly find ourselves in some weird position and wonder how did I get here, in a habit-energy way.
The model that they came up with to explain this quality of all this stuff that seems to be stored up in us, and did we put it all there ourselves, or did our parents put it there, or TV?
I mean, TV is an antiquated example now.
The social reality multiverse put it there.
What they conceived of is a vast storehouse.
Inside our hearts, inside our bodies, inside somewhere, we all carry around, or we are all inhabited by, a vast storehouse of potentials, of impulses, of energies, of tendencies, of memories.
And interestingly, all this is below our conscious awareness.
We can't directly see or know this vast storehouse.
They call the storehouse Alaya Vijnana in Sanskrit.
Alaya means storehouse and Vijnana means consciousness.
So the storehouse consciousness: there's this consciousness below the surface that stores all this stuff, stores it and stores it and stores it and stores it.
Now the idea of consciousness deserves a side note.
We tend to think of consciousness as me.
Consciousness as a process by which I think and understand myself moment to moment, right?
And when we think about consciousness, we think about one consciousness, or maybe we think about two, like conscious awareness, meaning there's some other stuff, subconscious.
But mostly we think about consciousness as me, as a single, event-driven thing, one thing happening after the next in consciousness.
They don't think about it that way.
They think about consciousness as an organic process that arises and passes away according to conditions, a kind of process that runs on stuff and has outputs that come out of it.
And in any given moment there's not just one consciousness but multiple consciousnesses operating all at the same time, in layers and patterns and combinations.
In any one moment there are always at least three consciousnesses going on at the same time, and sometimes up to eight.
In this model there are actually eight different consciousnesses.
Well, only one of them is the kind of mind that cognizes thought.
It's about getting into that too much in a half-hour talk.
We spent the whole weekend on this.
So have that in mind: consciousness as processes that are weaving together and running.
And this Alaya Vijnana consciousness, the storehouse consciousness, is running pretty much all the time, or actually, the way I think about this one, it's running all the time.
Some of them start and stop.
This one's running all the time, and it's always functioning so that it will always maintain conditions for these stored energies to be there waiting.
They actually called these stored things seeds.
So now I'm thinking about this like a vast underground farm, somewhere below my gut but infinite in size.
It's extremely fertile, but it's really dark down there.
It's the right kind of medium: warm, slightly moist, you know.
The right conditions for the seeds.
I mean, it's dry, I don't know.
The right conditions for the seeds just to be there waiting, waiting, waiting, waiting, waiting, waiting, waiting, until the conditions are right.
Then once in a while conditions open up a little crack somehow and let in a little light or a little rain or something, and the seeds germinate.
The seeds sprout.
And when these seeds sprout, what happens is we have experience.

The way they understand this is not like me, me, me, me, me having experiences, but in the vast [unclear: "door house"], moment after moment, conditions are shifting around, so the little rays of light are shining down there and seeds are sprouting and emerging and manifesting in a certain way in our awareness.
They say that every single experience we could have, including so-called physical experiences, is because of this process.
But it's much easier for us to understand if we think about this in terms of psychological experiences.
Love and hatred seem to be psychological experiences.
But let me give you a different example.
As I was preparing to try to lead this weekend retreat on this complicated model of consciousness, I experienced a lot of insecurity.
In the week, couple of weeks before it was to happen, I kept having thoughts and feelings that I would never be able to figure this out.
I would never be able to present it right.
Nobody would get it.
I'm not organized enough, or not good enough, or not capable enough to teach this material.
It just kept happening.
It was really destabilizing and demoralizing, and it made it hard to focus.
I'm trying to read this book, and meanwhile the mind is not processing the squiggles on the page to make words.
It's going you're not good enough, you're not good enough.
So you're not going to get this.
They're not going to understand it yet.
And of course I give myself a very high bar.
I don't want to just talk.
I want to have exercises and be really interesting.
And of course I want people to love me, and so on.
But eventually it occurred to me to actually apply what I was studying about consciousness to my own consciousness.
And I remembered, oh, this is what they're talking about.
Planted in my alaya vijnana, planted in my storehouse consciousness, are many seeds of anxiety, many seeds of inadequacy, many seeds of doubt, right?
And when conditions are right, those seeds are going to sprout.
And I thought, wow, these are really good conditions for those to sprout.
Preparing to give a major presentation, that's excellent for that.
The seeds are so happy: "God, it's just the right fertilizer.
Thank you.
I can grow really fast."
That really helped me, and I could start recognizing that these teachings say your experience is a result of a combination of conditions.
So these teachings do acknowledge that there are conditions happening.

Of course they say the conditions are because of consciousness, but in our case, since we're so convinced that there's an external reality, we can hold on to that conceit for now and say, okay, because the external reality is preparing to give a seminar, those are good conditions for these seeds to sprout.
But it's actually a two-way process.
Here's the good part: as the seeds are sprouting, according to the way we interact and respond to conditions, which is also influenced by the seeds that are sprouting, we plant new seeds.
So it's like a cycle.
Seeds sprout, new seeds are planted, seeds sprout, new seeds are planted, and conditions are changing.
The other piece of this, and here I had an opportunity, right: I could just plant more seeds, like, "Oh yeah, definitely, I'm canceling this thing right now.
Probably nobody's going to want to come anyway."
Actually, that thought did take hold for a while.
Or I could plant other seeds.
The first seed I could plant is the seed of mindful awareness.
Oh, this is an experience of anxiety.
This is an experience of fear.
Maybe it's to do with this seed thing, which is a sort of thought, an analytical thought.
But maybe that's a beneficial analytical thought, so I could plant that thought.
Maybe when anxiety arises I could plant with it the thought, oh, this is a seed sprouting.
Maybe that will help.
So the first is mindfulness, noticing what's happening, and the second is that I can plant a wholesome response.
I could plant: this will bring benefit to me and my dear friends, to teach this material.
Even though it's going to be hard and probably won't be any good, this will be better.
The seed of expectation of benefit, the seed of hope, the seed of faith, the seed of non-doubt, right?
So when seeds arise, we can recognize them as the arising of seeds, which immediately takes a lot of the pressure off, because there's a lot less me in that.
There's tremendously less me in "oh, conditions are right for anxiety to arise" versus "I'm so fucking anxious," right?
That's not my anxiety exactly, or even me being anxious, just anxiety arising makes sense.
And of course the conditions that support the arising and germinating of these seeds aren't always that obvious either, right?
Conditions are complex.
Cause and effect is very rich.
How many little inputs come into our senses in any given day?
Each one of them has a little causal effect, millions.

So even if we're not able to tell ourselves a reassuring story like I was able to tell myself, "oh, this is because X, Y and Z," we can still recognize all phenomena that arise in our heart, starting with emotional experience because it's easier for us.
Not as me, my problem, my fault, but as: oh, the arising, the emergence, the appearance of something.
Just that.
There it is.
Is it any different from a red car driving down the street, or a crow, or a raindrop, really?
So there's basically three things that happen in this model whenever we experience something.
First, we find out that there must have been a seed for that, down in the darkness where we couldn't see it.
Second, we find out there must be the right conditions for that seed to germinate.
And third, we recognize that there's another level of consciousness operating that's identifying with this.
That's telling us, this is you, here you are, this is you.
And we can also practice mindfulness with the identification itself.
Oh, there's anxiety arising, and identification with the anxiety.
There's a whole lot more to it, of course, but that's more or less the basic idea, as my limited, somewhat anxious understanding will allow me to express.
But where do these seeds come from?
Are they my fault?
Did I make some mistakes earlier that reinforced them, so that I plant all these seeds and now you reap what you sow?
Or maybe it's bigger than that.
Maybe it's bigger than just me, again.
When they arise and when I meet the manifestation of seeds, I do have a little moment of choice there, probably on a good day.
I have some influence.
I'm not without responsibility, but maybe it's not my fault, not exactly my fault.
I want to give you a little bit more.
We have just enough time, I think, to get a little more flavor of these teachings.
There are lengthy texts on all this, very long.
Not all of them have been translated, and they're really hard to read.
I've tried to read little bits of them and quickly gave up.
But a famous tradition in Buddhism in general, and especially in these Yogacara teachings, is to write verses.
First you write the six hundred page tome, and then you write the 20 verses, the 30 verses that sum it up, and then you write a commentary in the verses to explain what you meant.
As far as we know, this was first done by a fourth century Indian pundit named Vasubandhu, who wrote famous verses on this model of consciousness, the Yogacara model of consciousness.
And they must be really hard to understand, because I have not been able to find an English translation of these verses.
He wrote 30 verses and then 20 verses, so there's 50 verses.
And then a little bit later, a wonderful seventh century Chinese pilgrim named [unclear: "Zhuansong"].
And Zhuansong is a great character, you should learn about Zhuansong sometime.
There'll be another series of talks, maybe.
There had been a limited amount of Buddhism transmitted to China in the fifth and sixth centuries.
In the seventh century some of the monks and nuns were like, "This doesn't seem quite complete.
I don't get it.
We need to go back to the source."
And he's one of them who actually ignored an imperial edict and snuck out of China and went to India for 17 years, walking, collecting materials, studying with people.
He really loved this Yogacara teaching too, so he brought it all back to China and got it all translated into Chinese, and he also wrote verses.
And then, fast forwarding a little bit, to the 20th century, to [unclear: "Nan Han"], who memorized Vasubandhu's verses, I think in Chinese.
That's part of his monastic education.
He wrote his own verses.
I think he might have actually written them in English, which is interesting, like his third language.
So I'm going to read you a few of his verses, and then I'll carry on the tradition by commenting on his verses.
This is the first six verses of his 50 verse poem about this model, part one, the store consciousness.
*First, one mind is a field in which every kind of seed is sown.
This mind field can also be called "all the seeds."

In us are infinite varieties of seeds: seeds of samsara, nirvana, delusion and enlightenment; seeds of suffering, seeds of happiness; seeds of perception, name and word; seeds that manifest as body and mind, as realms of being, stages and worlds.
All are stored in our consciousness.
That is why it is called "store."
Some seeds are innate, handed down by our ancestors.
Some are sown while we are still in the womb.
Some were sown when we were children, whether transmitted by family, friends, society or education.
All our seeds are by nature individual and collective.
The quality of our life depends on the quality of the seeds that lie deep in our consciousness.*
So it appears we didn't do all this, he says.
In here the seeds are from our ancestors.
We receive them in the womb, we receive them as children, we receive them from society.
They're all in there, in vast numbers, more seeds than ever could sprout in one lifetime, which is why this is a multi-lifetime kind of model.
The seeds will continue to be planted and germinating through time.
But as they do, we're the one who is there at the intersection between conditions and sprouting seeds.
We're the one who can plant seeds of love, or at least understand the seeds of hate as they arise, so they don't do so much damage.

And as we gain some feeling for that in ourselves, we can look at others with compassionate eyes, with sympathetic eyes: even the most strange and warped and confused among us is also participating in this dance of the deep mind consciousness, seeds germinating and manifesting.
And of course it is our responsibility, just as it is their responsibility, to dance with that as best they can.
But who are we to know what seeds are arising in them in that moment, whether seeing them walking down the street or on national TV?
And then we all have wholesome seeds, seeds like faith.
I know Andrea in her talk talked a bit about faith or trust.
Wholesome seeds like energy, generosity, forgiveness: we all have these seeds.
And we all have the unwholesome seeds too: hatred, anger, judgment, ill will.
When these seeds manifest in different combinations, they become racism and war.
They become walking into the Macy's in Burlington and shooting people.
They become a life devoted to service.
They become all kinds of things.
They become everything that could ever become.
So, give myself a moment of compassion, [unclear: "killer prepare too many remarks"] here.
Hold on a sec, try to wrap this up.

So anyway, it's a deeper idea, I think, than some of our ideas about ourselves and each other, even some of the more nuanced ideas like "love the person but not the behavior," right, that kind of thing.
There's deeper and more complex dynamics at work here, and a healthy respect for the mystery of it all is a part of this model.
You can never directly see these seeds.
You can't go down there in the dark with a flashlight, no matter how many clever therapists you hire.
But you can become curious about the patterns of manifestation, and you can be as wise and kind and compassionate as you can.
You can seek support, you can seek love, you can let love be our legacy.
So I'll close with a Zen story.
Little Zen stories tell about this in very simple ways.
This is the seventh case in the Gateless Gate collection that a few of us have been studying together.
Very simple, but it has this whole thing in it, I think.
One time a monk said to the teacher Zhaozhou, "I have just entered the monastery.
Please teach me."
Zhaozhou said, "Have you eaten your rice gruel?"
The monk said, "Yes, I have."
Zhaozhou said, "Please wash your bowl."
The monk understood.
So: I see you and I care.
I'm going to show myself.
I've just entered the monastery, here I am, this one here.
I'm willing to ask for connection, I'm willing to be curious, I'm willing to ask for help.
Please teach me.
Oh, I see you.
I see you.
Have you eaten?
Have you eaten?
Are you okay?
Do you have what you need?
Have you eaten?
Yes, I have.
I meet your interest.
I'm willing to be here with you.
Yes, I have.
Then I honor you.
I honor you, I offer you all my love and support, and I want to remind you that you can take care of yourself.
Please wash your bowl.
Just take care of it.
Wash your bowl.

And here's the thing: when we feel the vastness of this [unclear: "alive Vijnana"], when we wash our bowl, we realize we're washing everybody's bowl, and we're washing the feet of beggars, and we're washing the counters, and we're washing the world.
We're washing love over the planet, just washing our bowl.
Sometimes this looks like going to Baton Rouge to help with flood relief.
One of our members did that recently.
That's love.
Other times it looks like coming to the Zendo every week to rest in our breathing and silently support each other.
That's love too.
Other times we're overcome by the fruits of these seeds.
It's too much sometimes.
Of course, how would it not be too much sometimes, right?
Of course the storehouse is vast, and it's full of some really tough seeds.
There's some tough stuff down there, and tough conditions will bring it out.

Luckily we can help each other, and little by little we can feel into this rich interplay that's so much bigger than me or you, and is me and you, and is everything, and that everything we do really is about love.
So that's my attempt to bring love and Yogacara together.
So, thanks.
